method: Scope was assigned only where a publisher, journal, or university repository supplied a sufficiently specific abstract describing the work's actual treatment. Titles alone and third-party summaries were not treated as sufficient evidence.
policy: These notes support work-level scope classification only. They make no claim about complete object extraction, preferred readings, identity, rights, or permission to reproduce text or images.

entries.finding: The Oxford University Press abstract says the article uses bowl orthography as early evidence for the Babylonian Hebrew vocalization tradition and analyzes characteristic vowel and spelling features.

The Cambridge University Press abstract describes a philological re-examination of obscure passages, new lexemes and meanings in the Aramaic bowls; it also notes a preliminary edition of Nippur 12 N 387, but the stated organizing purpose is linguistic.
The Ca' Foscari repository abstract says the article studies the use of Ephesians 6:10-17 on IBC 3 and uses it to discuss biblical citation and religious identification in late-antique magic.
The Ca' Foscari repository abstract describes an analysis of Northern Mesopotamian demons on one bowl and their possible implications for the afterlife of Hatrene inhabitants and cults.

The journal abstract says the article compares late-antique double-bowl sets with earlier Mesopotamian double-jar burials and proposes that the bowl configuration symbolically buried hostile entities.
The University of Groningen abstract describes a study of orality, textuality and performative utterances across bowl spells, arguing for a transfer of performativity from speech to writing.
The Brill abstract says the article compares examples of lost midrashim in the New Testament and Aramaic bowls to demonstrate the bowls' significance for early Jewish literature.
The University of Catania abstract describes a linguistic and cultural reconsideration of how a Jewish divorce formula was translated and adapted in a series of Syriac bowl spells.

The Wiley abstract defines the late-antique Aramaic incantation-text corpus, surveys its religious content, and identifies the field's major questions about language, identity, literacy, praxis and demonology.

The Oxford University Press abstract says the article re-analyzes and newly interprets one previously published Iraq Museum bowl, IM 9736, including a fresh reading that identifies it as a separation spell.
The Oxford University Press abstract presents and analyzes the six-part text of one bowl, Moussaieff 164, including its adjurations, threats, biblical verses and literary parallels.
